extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students of American government and colonial history
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes and analyzes political, judicial, municipal, and social institutions in British North American colonies (representation, legislatures, courts, local government, social classes, political thought, and early federation attempts). Intended as a textbook account for students and general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonial representation was organized by differing territorial units (town, county, parish) rather than by equal-population districts; charters often fixed numbers (e.g., Rhode Island: Newport not more than six persons; Providence, Portsmouth, Warwick four each; others two). Massachusetts originally provided two representatives per town but allowed the assembly to alter numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that equal representation principle was not accepted; practical attempts were made to give special recognition to more populous areas. Examples: New England—town as unit; middle colonies—county as unit; South Carolina—parishes with widely varying populations leading to unequal representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial legislative powers (scope and character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonial assemblies claimed entire and exclusive authority to regulate domestic concerns, especially taxation, and often asserted strong legislative power in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charters conferred general legislative power (example: Massachusetts charter of 1691: assembly had 'full power and authority... to make, ordain, and establish all manner of wholesome and reasonable orders, laws, statutes, and ordinances... so that the same be not repugnant or contrary to the laws of this our realm of England'). Assemblies also exercised control over the executive by withholding salaries of officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal limitations on colonial legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite broad assertions of legislative power, colonial legislatures faced legal limitations such as gubernatorial vetoes, requirement to send laws to England for royal approval in most colonies, and Parliamentary acts rendering colonial laws repugnant to English laws null and void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific exceptions noted: Maryland, Rhode Island, and Connecticut did not require sending laws to England. Courts sometimes declared colonial laws void on constitutional or common-right grounds (e.g., South Carolina court nullified a 1712 act on Magna Charta/common right). Later Parliamentary assertions declared colonies subordinate in all cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial judiciary organization and jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonial courts were hierarchical: justices of the peace (local, limited civil/criminal jurisdiction), county courts (criminal jurisdiction except capital cases, civil jurisdiction for larger amounts), and high courts (appeals from lower courts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justices of the peace were generally governor-appointed and handled small civil claims (e.g., under five pounds in New York, under forty shillings in Massachusetts). High courts' composition varied (royal colonies: governor as chancellor + council; Massachusetts: chief justice + four associates). Appeals could be taken to the king in council in England with monetary thresholds (Pennsylvania: >50 pounds; Georgia: >500 pounds). Elective judiciary was rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal corporations: form and powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately twenty municipal corporations existed, chartered by colonial governors; governing bodies followed English models (common council: mayor, recorder, aldermen, councillors). Franchise and selection methods varied; mayor often appointed by governor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many cities councilmen and aldermen were elected by a restricted franchise excluding full manhood suffrage; some councils were closed corporations with life terms and vacancy-filling powers (Philadelphia, Annapolis, Norfolk). Municipal charters conferred somewhat restricted powers initially; later special acts from colonial assemblies expanded powers. Notable feature: fusion of executive, legislative, and judicial functions in municipal bodies (commission form parallels this fusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rural local government units and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Local government differed regionally: New England—town as primary unit governed by town meeting of electors (choose officers, levy taxes, pass by-laws); middle colonies—combination of town and county with county boards/supervisors absorbing administrative functions; South—county/parish-based administration due to plantation settlement patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New England counties were mainly for judicial purposes. Middle-colony county boards (e.g., created c.1691 in New York) modeled later western state local government. Southern counties' officers (county lieutenant, sheriff, justices of the peace, coroners) were often governor-appointed, producing self-perpetuating planter elites controlling county administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social class structure in colonial society
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear economic/social stratification: upper class (clergy, professionals, merchants, landed proprietors/planters), middle class (small farmers, traders, storekeepers), lower class (slaves, poor whites, mechanics, indentured servants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with New York example: manorial families (Livingstons, Van Rensselaers, etc.) formed an entrenched landed aristocracy; rich merchants formed another elite; indentured Irish and German servants and imported labor augmented lower ranks; advertisements for runaway servants and slaves illustrate the mixed labor population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial political theory and attitudes toward democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonists, including educated and well-to-do, generally lacked enthusiasm for abstract democracy; Puritan resistance targeted royal prerogative rather than equality. Some democratic practices existed locally, but many restrictions (e.g., freeman status tied to church membership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: John Wise's 1717 discussion enumerates forms (democracy, aristocracy, monarchy) and conditions for a democracy (assigned time/place for assembly; majority vote rules; appointment of magistrates). John Cotton (1644) called democracy 'the meanest and worst of all forms of government.' The Puritan requirement that freemen be church members illustrates limits to democratic inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious toleration and limits on suffrage
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious liberty in the colonies was limited; toleration developed gradually but exclusions existed (e.g., Catholics and Jews excluded from suffrage in New York by law; Virginia's established church sought to suppress dissent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical enforcement varied and disfranchisement may not always have been consistently applied. James Madison cited prosecutions for publishing religious opinions (men jailed as late as 1774). Reference to scholarship on the rise of religious liberty in America provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments in intercolonial federation
rubrics_metrics.description: There were three notable pre-Revolutionary federation attempts: New England Confederation (1643) for mutual defence and welfare; Albany conference (1754) where Franklin led a committee proposing union (rejected by colonists and the crown); Stamp Act Congress (1765) where nine colonies convened to protest the Stamp Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New England Confederation lasted ~20 years but left little permanent impression. Albany plan feared by colonists (would give crown too much power) and by crown (too democratic). Stamp Act Congress produced addresses and petitions rather than permanent union; repeal of Stamp Act halted union momentum until the Revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committees of correspondence and revolutionary organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Committees of correspondence were local groups selected to correspond, compare views, and cooperate against British policy; they became key vehicles for revolutionary organization, popular education, and mobilization (e.g., Boston committee under Samuel Adams, 1772).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local committees multiplied rapidly and operated under county committees, forming a parallel government structure ('a government within a government'). They called conventions, selected delegates, supervised boycotts, and assumed reins of local revolutionary activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of selecting delegates and instructions for Continental Congresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection methods for congressional delegates varied widely (chosen by colonial assemblies, town meetings, committees of correspondence, county conventions, general meetings); instructions given to delegates typically authorized consultation on colonial grievances and recommended measures short of declaring independence at early stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Pennsylvania—chosen by colonial assembly; New Hampshire—delegates selected by town-appointed delegates; Connecticut—elected by committees of correspondence; New Jersey/Delaware/Maryland/Virginia—by county conventions; South Carolina/North Carolina—general meetings. Early instructions emphasized remonstrance and reconciliation; later instructions grew firmer, authorizing measures to secure redress and protect American rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement mechanisms for collective colonial actions (boycott enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress recommended committees in every county, city, and town to observe conduct regarding the non-importation association, publish names of violators, and enable local tribunals to act against those violating the boycott—thus creating a test of allegiance and local enforcement apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These committees were instructed to publicize violators so they would be 'universally contemned' and to authorize tribunals competent to deal with refractory citizens. The text notes that such measures effectively 'burned their bridges' by creating institutions and practices that committed communities to revolutionary policies.
